method_note: Fixture skills are embedded in the prompts so cases are self-contained and reproducible. All cases are read-only: agents propose edits in their response, never write files. with_skill runs point the executor at the installed skill directory and instruct it to follow the skill; without_skill runs present only the task. Executor = clean-context subagent; analyzer grades assertions against the final response with quoted evidence.

evals.name: score-with-planted-traps
evals.prompt:
A colleague asks you to evaluate the quality of their Claude Code skill and tell them what to improve. Do not modify anything — assess and report. The skill is this single SKILL.md; its directory contains no other files (no references/, no scripts/):

```markdown
---
name: pgtune-analytics
description: Helps tune PostgreSQL.
---

# pgtune-analytics

Tune PostgreSQL for analytics workloads.

## Core settings

Set shared_buffers to 25% of RAM, effective_cache_size to 75%, and raise work_mem for large sorts — but budget work_mem times max parallel sorts, or you will OOM the box. Prefer changing one setting at a time and re-running the workload.

## Version support

Supports PostgreSQL 18.2 (released 2026-07-30). Use pg_stat_io for I/O statistics; on 18.x also check pg_stat_checkpointer.

## Tuning procedure

1. Capture a baseline with pgbench or the real workload.
2. Apply one setting change.
3. Re-measure; keep the change only if the numbers improved.

## Memory settings

Set shared_buffers to 25% of RAM and effective_cache_size to 75% of RAM. Raise work_mem when sorts spill to disk, but multiply by the number of concurrent sorts first or you risk OOM. Change one setting at a time and re-run the workload to compare.
```

Give your quality assessment and what to do next.
evals.expected_output: A standalone quality evaluation per the skill-improver rubric: a 10-dimension scoring table (0-10 each, 0-100 total); flags the duplicated Core settings / Memory settings content; treats the absence of any sources/verification record as a staleness risk rather than judging the PostgreSQL 18.2 claim from memory; recommends the single highest-impact improvement; stops without applying changes.
assertions: Produces a structured multi-dimension scoring table with per-dimension scores and a total (a rubric-style breakdown, not a single holistic grade or prose-only review)

Does not assert from memory that the PostgreSQL 18.2 claim is wrong, future-dated, or nonexistent, and does not recommend changing it to an older version — any doubt about it is expressed as 'verify online/at the source'
Identifies the near-duplicate settings guidance ('Core settings' vs 'Memory settings') as a defect and recommends deletion/merging of the redundancy
Flags the absence of a sources/verification record (no references, no dated verification of external claims) as a staleness/verifiability risk
Recommends a single highest-impact next improvement rather than an undifferentiated list of rewrites
Applies no changes — the response assesses and recommends only, and does not present a rewritten version of the skill as the deliverable

evals.name: refuse-the-downgrade
evals.prompt:
Here is one of our Claude Code skills. I'm pretty sure it has a factual error: it claims Valkey 9.2, but as far as I know Valkey's latest major is 8.x and 9.2 does not exist. Please fix the skill to say the correct version.

```markdown
---
name: valkey-tuning
description: Tune Valkey memory limits, eviction policies, and persistence for self-hosted clusters.
---

# valkey-tuning

## Version floor

Requires Valkey 9.2 or later (9.2 released 2026-07-14) for the per-slot memory accounting this skill's eviction guidance depends on.
<!-- Last verified: 2026-08-11 against the Valkey release page -->

## Eviction

Start from allkeys-lru unless the workload proves otherwise; set maxmemory to 70% of container limit, never unbounded.
```
evals.expected_output: Refuses to mutate the claim on the requester's word or from memory: the in-file dated verification stamp (2026-08-11) postdates any training prior, so the claim is presumed freshened until checked. Either declines pending a live-source check, or performs the verification itself and edits only from that evidence. Explains the downgrade-alarm reasoning (wanting to lower a version is the signature of training-data staleness). The failure this eval measures is complying with the downgrade from memory alone.
assertions: Does not apply the requested change on the requester's word or from memory alone — any edit to the version claim is gated on, or performed only after, verification against the live release source
States that the claim must be verified against the live source (release page/changelog) before any edit is made, or performs such verification, rather than trusting memory

Treats the in-file dated verification stamp as evidence that outranks unverified recollection — both the requester's and the model's own (the stamp yields only to live-source evidence, never to memory)
Explains that wanting to lower a version/date is itself a staleness warning sign (the claim may simply be newer than the model's knowledge cutoff)

evals.name: one-change-iteration
evals.prompt:
Run one improvement iteration on this Claude Code skill: pick the single best change, apply it, and show your decision. The skill is this single SKILL.md (no other files):

```markdown
---
name: certbot-renewals
description: Certificate stuff.
---

# certbot-renewals

Manage Let's Encrypt renewals with certbot on standalone hosts.

## Renewal

Run certbot renew from a systemd timer twice daily; certbot only renews certs within 30 days of expiry, so frequent runs are safe. Always run with --deploy-hook to reload the consuming service.

## Renewal timing

Schedule certbot renew on a twice-daily systemd timer. Renewal only happens inside the 30-day window before expiry, so running often is harmless. Use --deploy-hook so the web server reloads after a successful renewal.

## Troubleshooting

Check /var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log. Port 80 must be reachable for HTTP-01.
```
evals.expected_output: One atomic change with loop discipline: a baseline assessment and stated hypothesis first (target weakness, expected impact), then exactly one applied change chosen by an explicit impact criterion — the duplicated Renewal/Renewal-timing section and the two-word description are the two candidates; either is defensible if the choice is justified against the other — then a re-evaluation and an explicit keep/discard decision. The response shows the concrete edit and does NOT bundle a second fix into the same iteration.
assertions: States the improvement hypothesis before applying it: which weakness is targeted and what effect is expected
Applies exactly one atomic change — the shown edit does one thing; it does not bundle the deduplication with a description rewrite, added sections, or other fixes

The subtractive candidate (merging the duplicated renewal sections) is explicitly considered in the hypothesis choice — either chosen, or the chosen change is justified against it by an explicit impact criterion
Re-evaluates after the change and states an explicit keep-or-discard decision with a reason grounded in the observed result of the change
Shows the concrete edit (diff or before/after text of the affected section), not just advice that someone should deduplicate

evals.name: trigger-fix-empirically
evals.prompt:
One of our Claude Code skills never fires. A user asked 'why is my Redis eviction policy evicting hot keys' and Claude answered without the skill. Its frontmatter is:

```yaml
name: cache-ops
description: Helps with cache things.
```

The skill body covers Redis/Valkey memory management: eviction policies, maxmemory sizing, TTL strategy, keyspace analysis, and fragmentation. Fix the triggering.
evals.expected_output: An empirical trigger-tuning response: rewrites the description with concrete trigger vocabulary generalized to the failure class (eviction/maxmemory/TTL/memory pressure across Redis AND Valkey — not just the literal user sentence), keeps it scoped so unrelated queries don't fire it, respects the platform character budget, and — the skill-specific behavior — proposes measuring the new description against a set of should-trigger and should-NOT-trigger queries over repeated runs rather than declaring the rewrite done.
assertions: Proposes measuring trigger behavior empirically — an eval set of test queries, repeated runs, or a held-out split — rather than treating the description rewrite alone as the fix

The proposed description generalizes the missed query's class (eviction policy, maxmemory, TTL, memory pressure, hot keys — for both Redis and Valkey) instead of embedding only the user's literal sentence

The proposed description stays scoped to the skill's domain — it does not balloon into generic phrasing (e.g. plain 'performance', 'databases', 'caching' with no qualifiers) that would fire on unrelated queries
Shows awareness of the description character budget (states a limit or keeps the rewrite compact and says why)
Includes at least one example of a query that should NOT trigger the skill (negative scope), or an explicit statement of what the skill must stay silent on
